title: Mitochondrial network remodeling and the glutamine-proline axis in pulmonary vascular disease associated with CHD.
text:
(Project #3)
The incidence of congenital heart defects in the U.S. is ~1 per 100 live births, and approximately 50% of these
children require medical and/or surgical attention. Although survival for these children has improved, they
continue to suffer significant morbidity and late mortality, in part because of abnormal vascular reactivity within
their lungs. Our studies are designed to increase our understanding of the mitochondrial network dynamics in
this process, which could improve the survival of children born with congenital heart defects.

title: Intravascular microstructural, chemical and biomechanical characterization of coronary plaques
text:
The most prevalent type of heart disease is caused by atherosclerosis, the thickening of the vessel wall
and creation of atherosclerotic plaque. In this project, we will develop an imaging tool for the compre-
hensive assessment of atherosclerotic plaque composition and vulnerability, with a clear pathway for
translation into the clinical environment to enable the determination of the optimal treatment strategy
in individual patients.

title: Lead Development & Optimization Shared Resource
text: LEAD DEVELOPMENT AND OPTIMIZATION SHARED RESOURCE (LDOSR): ABSTRACT The Lead Development and Optimization Shared Resource (LDOSR) is a shared resource of The University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC), composed of three component laboratories located on the KU Lawrence West Campus: High-Throughput Screening (HTS), Medicinal Chemistry (MDCM) and the Biopharmaceutical Innovation and Optimization Center (BIOC). LDOSR provides preferred access to KUCC members to accelerate projects from drug-target discovery through high-throughput screening, compound hit prioritization, secondary in vitro confirmatory assays, medical chemistry optimization, in vitro pharmacology testing, in vivo pharmacokinetics, and drug delivery formulations for in vivo preclinical proof-of-concept testing. The activities involved with the generation, evaluation, and optimization of drug candidates is an iterative process that crosses several scientific disciplines. The LDOSR has been structured to optimize services under a single, easy-to-access umbrella, with oversight from the Director and a team of project managers, allowing projects to move seamlessly between component laboratories. Comprehensive plans tailored to fit each project’s needs ensure users get the most relevant data to move their projects forward. Additionally, the LDOSR offers drop-in ready grant submission and publication language. Over the past five years (2016-2020), the LDOSR has supported 167 KUCC member projects (~76% were peer-review funded). The LDOSR leverages research infrastructure established, historically, through internationally recognized medicinal and pharmaceutical chemistry research conducted by the University of Kansas School of Pharmacy. Added to this is the availability of industry experienced scientists from former area Pharma and CRO companies. The LDOSR has successfully recruited top-notch scientists with industry and academic qualifications to lead and staff the three component laboratories. The LDOSR, working with the Associate Director for Translational Research, established the Drug Discovery and Development Steering Committee. This translational-research catalyst provides a forum for KUCC investigators to develop research concepts at the chemistry/biology interface with support from the LDO laboratories. The LDOSR partners with The Institute for Advancing Medical Innovation to advance drug discovery projects through early drug development, actively conducting and supporting studies necessary to enable first-in-human clinical trials. Additionally, LDOSR staff serve on the Investigator-Initiated Trial Steering Committee, which facilitates evaluation of development candidates in early phase experimental therapeutics trials conducted by the D3ET research program. Lastly, bioanalytical methods for determination of drug and metabolite concentrations in preclinical matrices, are transferred to the Clinical Pharmacology Shared Resource where they are cross-validated in human matrices under GLP conditions to support early phase clinical trials. The result is a fully integrated, end-to-end translational research function capable of advancing novel cancer therapeutic agents invented by KUCC members to clinical trials.

title: Brain Tumor SPORE Grant
text:
Despite the best efforts of neurosurgeons and neuro-oncologists, the incidence and mortality rates of brain
cancer have remained stable over the past 20 years. Unfortunately, in 2021 alone, more than 18,000 people
died of brain and other CNS tumors. Through the work proposed in this SPORE application, we will develop
noninvasive measures to improve our diagnosis and response-assessment and novel cellular immunotherapy to
improve the lives of individuals with brain cancer.

title: Regulatory mechanisms for retinal ganglion cell genesis
text:
This proposal is aimed at understanding how key regulators (transcription factors) interact with and modify the
epigenetic landscape and promote retinal ganglion cell differentiation. The findings from the proposed
experiments will lead to further insights into the molecular basis underpinning the generation of the cellular
diversity in the retina and offer guidance for developing strategies to treat degenerative retinal diseases.

title: High-Throughput 3D Multiscale Mass Spectrometry Imaging for Understanding Neurochemical Heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Novel mass spectrometry-based technologies will be developed to create molecular atlases of the
mouse brain impacted by Alzheimer’s Disease and healthy control. The proposed innovations in mass
spectrometry imaging and single-cell mass spectrometry measurements and multiscale data fusion, in
combination with unique mouse models of Alzheimer’s Disease, will reveal the temporal and spatial
signatures of neuronal vulnerability in Alzheimer’s Disease and the effects of hippocampal
neurogenesis on disease progression. The spatially and chemically resolved molecule portrait of
healthy and Alzheimer’s Disease impacted brains will help elucidate the molecular mechanisms of
disease progression and identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Deep learning based predictive analytics to improve patient health.
text:
The project focus on developing deep learning pipeline of methods including a missingness-
informed knowledge graph-based embedding method to improve patient representations, and a
graph convolutional networks (GCNs) based framework to integrate patient EHR embeddings
with other health determinants into a unified model for improved clinical risk prediction.

title: Characterization of a ubiquitin-independent pathway for proteasomal degradation
text:
Many diseases, including Azheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Huntington’s diseases, are caused by an abnormal
accumulation of proteins, yet the pathways that degrade proteins are not fully understood. The goal of this
proposal is to characterize a ubiquitin-independent protein degradation pathway that may be involved in
degrading misfolded and/or oxidatively-damaged proteins. This work will provide fundamental insights into
protein degradation and may lead to new methods for treating diseases caused by aberrant proteins.

title: Molecular imaging and therapy in aortic valve calcification
text:
The VA patient population is characterized by a high prevalence of aortic stenosis. By developing new imaging
tools to track disease progression and identifying new treatments, this project will help improve the
management of patients with calcific aortic stenosis. Ultimately, this will improve the health of veterans and
reduce healthcare costs.

title: Decoding the Cell-specific Impact of Epigenomic and Alternative Splicing Regulation during T1D Progression
text:
Project Narrative.
The progression of type 1 diabetes (T1D) is influenced by both intrinsic and environmental signals. Our
proposal involves utilizing single nucleus transcriptome and chromatin profiling, along with human pluripotent
stem cell models, to thoroughly investigate how these factors affect the function, and survival of human
pancreatic β cells in both healthy and diseased states. Gaining a deeper understanding of the roles played by
intrinsic and environmental signals will greatly improve our knowledge of β cell destruction during T1D
progression, which will ultimately pave the way for developing precision therapy for T1D patients.

title: The role of APP in neurogenesis and AD in Down syndrome
text:
This project examines the role of amyloid precursor protein overexpression in cortical
malformation and Alzheimer’s disease in Down syndrome using induced pluripotent
stem cells of Down syndrome that were edited to eliminate one APP allele.

title: NAc Circuits Underlying Opioid Taking and Seeking
text:
The goal of this proposal is to determine the cell types and circuits that are active in the nucleus accumbens
during opioid taking and seeking, and how these cells and circuits adapt during chronic opioid consumption.
These findings will provide a more granular understanding of opioid induced changes in reward circuitry and
inform the development of targeted interventions to combat opioid addiction and its long-term consequences.

title: Machine Learning to Disentangle Neurobiological Heterogeneity in the Schizophrenia Spectrum Disease Course
text:
Schizophrenia is a neuropsychiatric disorder which likely implicates network-based dysfunction in hetero-
geneous ways that have thus far been difficult to disentangle using traditional approaches to neuroimaging
analyses in human subjects. Innovative, discovery-driven machine learning approaches have recently shown
potential to discover latent neurobiological patterns within the schizophrenia spectrum, identifying potential
epicenters of disease and patterns of disease progression. This proposal will apply one such method –
Subtype and Stage Inference – to probe differential patterns of disease progression in the anterior and
posterior hippocampal-cortical networks with the goal of identifying neurobiological subtypes of disease in the
schizophrenia population.

title: Designer extracellular vesicles for cancer therapy
text:
This project is aimed to translate our engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) into effective cancer therapy. We
will optimize cytotoxicity and immune stimulatory functions of DR5 agonistic scFvs armed EVs and test these
designer EVs in mouse clinical trials. We will then optimize bioprocessing and standardize workflow for the
EVs production. This work will prepare our designer EVs to be explored as an alternative therapy for CAR-T
cells.

title: CD8 T cell derived Granzyme K activates complement that drives synovial fibroblast inflammation
text:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a disease that affects the joints and is characterized by chronic
inflammation, cartilage and bone damage that and can lead to permanent disability. We are
studying how a type of white blood cell (CD8 T cell) and a protein called a granzyme can
activate an inflammatory pathway (called the complement pathway) which drives inflammation
and joint damage. Defining this new pathway would reveal new targets for drug development to
treat RA.

title: Extraction and summarization of evidence-based medicine
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it transforms free-text clinical evidence in the
literature into a computable format that can better support evidence extraction and summarization. It applies
natural language processing to unstructured biomedical literature to support evidence-based clinical research
and to enhance the health of the public. The proposed research is also relevant to the part of the NLM's strategic
plan that focuses on (1) development and demonstration of innovative informatics methods and data science
techniques for informing public health, (2) advanced information retrieval and knowledge discovery from very
large and/or heterogeneous data sets

title: Identifying a transcriptional core regulatory circuitry and other critical transcription factor dependencies in H3.3 G34R/V high-grade glioma
text:
High-grade gliomas of the cerebral cortex are intractable brain tumors with a 5-year survival of less than 20%.
Recurrent Gly34Arg/Val substitutions in Histone H3.3 (H3.3 G34R/V) occur in more than 15% of cerebral cortex
high-grade gliomas found in adolescents and young adults. This proposal aims to determine the impact of H3.3
G34R/V mutations on transcriptional regulatory patterns contributing to tumorigenesis and identify critical
transcription factor dependencies by leveraging a novel collection of primary tumors, patient-derived orthotopic
xenografts, and a range of patient-derived cell lines modeling wild-type, H3.3 G34R/V mutant, and CRISPR-
corrected H3.3 G34R/V backgrounds.

title: Mammal-virus evolution from global to local scales
text:
Recent outbreaks of Ebola, monkeypox, and SARS-related CoVs all originated in wild mammals, increasing the
societal need to identify predictive rules of cross-species viral transmission (or ‘spillover’). To address gaps in
mammal-virus knowledge, my research program will build automated tools for curating public genetic and
phylogenetic data, including a pipeline for re-inferring global mammal phylogeny; apply the taxonomically
updated data from our tools to test the sensitivity of species-level spillover risk models globally; and investigate
the extent to which rates of gene flow predict viral sharing among wild rodent populations in Arizona. By unifying
perspectives across scales, this research advances understandings of how and why viral spillover occurs.

title: NMDAR contributions to cognitive-emotional prefrontal circuits in aging
text:
REVISED
Cognitive decline affects the quality of life for millions of aging Americans and is a prominent feature of Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD), but the neural mechanisms that drive cognitive decline are not fully understood. This study will examine how the expression and functional contributions of the NMDA receptor, a critical circuit substrate for learning and memory, are altered among cognitive-emotional prefrontal circuits during aging in a well-established non-human primate model. Our findings will also reveal how extrasynaptic NMDA receptor expression across heterogeneous prefrontal circuits may confer vulnerability to age-related decline, and guide the advancement of more targeted therapeutic strategies for aging and ADRD.

title: Bioscience Screening
text: The Bioscience Screening Shared Resource (BS-SR) provides SCI members with the ability to conduct high- throughput chemical, siRNA, cDNA, and high-content screens for the purpose of drug discovery and target identification. The BS-SR incorporates instrumentation (purchased with NCRR NIH Instrumentation grants S10RR019513, S10RR026338, S10OD025004, and S10OD026899), databases, and compound and molecular libraries to allow SCI members to discover novel molecular targets and identify small molecules that modulate them. The BS-SR provides access to a fully automated confocal High-Content fluorescent microplate imager with live cell, fluidics, and phase contrast options, advanced microplate 96- and 384-well head pipetting liquid handlers, and fluorescence, luminescence, and absorbance multimode microplate readers. The BS-SR has over 130,000 small molecules for compound screens, 15,000 human cDNAs for genomic screens, and whole-genome siRNA libraries targeting the human genome (the siARRAY whole human genome siRNA library from Dharmacon targeting 21,000 human genes) and the mouse genome (Qiagen mouse whole-genome siRNA set V1 against 22,000 genes). Access to the equipment and services are provided efficiently and cost-effectively through the BS-SR. The BS-SR provides access to new technologies, such as high-throughput organoid screens and other services to meet the evolving needs of SCI members. Members of all programs use the BS-SR, with the heaviest use coming from the Cancer Biology and Cancer Stem Cells and Cancer Therapeutics programs. The BS-SR participated in nine cancer-focused publications (2 high-impact). The BS-SR will become part of the new University-led Innovative Medicine Accelerator. Some major investments have already been made (e.g., 2500 FDA-approved drugs or drugs in clinical trials library) to ensure outstanding support for SCI members in the future. The annual budget of the BS-SR is $404,790, yet the CCSG request is $104,174. Accordingly, the BS-SR leverages institutional support and seeks 26% from CCSG funds, which is anticipated to decrease once BS-SR merges with the new Innovative Medicine Accelerator High-Throughput Screening Knowledge Center. The BS-SR is focused on three major scientific aims: (1) to allow access to state-of-the-art screening technologies, (2) to provide data analysis and consultation for high-throughput screens, and (3) to provide cost- effective and expeditious screening services.
